summary: A puzzle of distrust and curiosity, in which grief, hatred, and outrage at a child-killer who escaped the law move twelve avengers and a detective's conscience.

hungry.why: Meals in the restaurant car structure the days, but no one hungers.

sleepy.why: Ratchett is drugged with barbital before he is stabbed, Poirot lies awake hearing a groan and a bell, and every alibi is about who slept and who woke in the night.

nauseous.why: No one is sickened; even the corpse with twelve wounds is examined calmly by Dr Constantine.

fatigued.why: No one exerts themselves; the train sits in the snow.

pain.why: Ratchett, drugged with barbital, is stabbed twelve times and probably felt little; pain belongs to the past crime, not to the train.

disgusted.why: Poirot refuses Ratchett because he does not like his face, and every passenger speaks of Cassetti, the child-killer, with revulsion.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The train is stalled in a snowdrift between Vincovci and Brod, the heating is discussed, and the snow outside closes the world of suspects.

afraid.why: Ratchett shows Poirot threatening letters and offers twenty thousand dollars for protection, and Mrs Hubbard plays terror at the man she claims hid in her compartment.

anxious.why: Mary Debenham, overheard saying not now, when it's all over, frets at every delay, and the conspirators sweat through Poirot's interviews as their stories crack.

panic.why: Mrs Hubbard's shrieks about a man in her compartment are theatre, and when the truth comes out no one bolts; the snow leaves nowhere to run.

sensory-pleasures.why: Poirot enjoys his dinners and the train's comforts, which is all the senses get.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The passengers' reading and the red kimono are props, not pleasures; no one enjoys art.

fun-excitement.why: No one plays; the puzzle is work for Poirot and dread for the rest.

love-romantic.why: Colonel Arbuthnot and Mary Debenham hide their attachment, the Count shields his wife Helena, and Hardman was in love with the maid Susanne who killed herself.

love-family.why: Twelve people bound to the Armstrong family, Daisy's grandmother and aunt, her nurse and governess, and the father of the maid who died, avenge the murdered child together.

grief.why: Every conspirator carries grief for Daisy, for Sonia Armstrong who died bearing a stillborn child, for the colonel who shot himself, and for Susanne the maid.

missing-someone.why: The conspirators speak of little Daisy, Sonia, and the colonel as people whose absence has shaped their lives since.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Poirot and his old friend M. Bouc work the case together over meals, and the twelve conspirators are bound by friendship and service to the Armstrongs.

empathy.why: Poirot reads each passenger's distress during the interviews, and at the end weighs the conspirators' suffering in deciding which solution to present.

compassion.why: Poirot and Bouc choose the solution that spares the twelve, Greta Ohlsson devotes her life to mission children, and the group shields the Countess from exposure.

grateful.why: Linda Arden's eyes fill when Poirot offers the first solution, but gratitude is unspoken as the case closes.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Poirot takes satisfaction in solving Bouc's problem, but the help he gives at the end is mercy rather than pleasure.

trustful-distrustful.why: Every passenger lies about identity or alibi, Poirot distrusts each story and sets traps, and Ratchett trusted no one, keeping a loaded pistol under his pillow.

depressed.why: Linda Arden says the Armstrong murders broke her and the household; the conspirators' grief has had years to settle into something like despair.

angry.why: Colonel Arbuthnot flushes with anger when Poirot presses Mary Debenham, and the conspirators' fury at Cassetti's acquittal is the motive for twelve blows.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship rank at stake.

hatred.why: All twelve hate Cassetti, who kidnapped and killed Daisy, caused her mother's and father's deaths, and bought his way out of an American court.

contempt.why: Poirot turns down Ratchett's money with open contempt, and Princess Dragomiroff looks down on everyone, including Poirot's investigation.

resentment.why: Cassetti escaped the law through money and influence, and twelve people who loved the Armstrongs form themselves into a jury to give him the sentence he dodged.

proud.why: Poirot preens over his little grey cells as he unravels the plot, and Princess Dragomiroff declares with pride that she would have struck Cassetti herself.

amused.why: Mrs Hubbard's garrulous turns and Poirot's teasing of M. Bouc lighten the inquiry, and Poirot enjoys the joke of the too-many clues.

sense-of-belonging.why: The passengers seem a random mix of nationalities and classes, but all twelve belong to one group, the Armstrong household and its friends, acting as a jury.

lonely.why: The Countess and the others have lived for years with a secret, and Hardman lost the woman he loved, but loneliness is not dwelt on.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The twelve appoint themselves jury and executioner of a child murderer the law let go, and Poirot must judge whether to hand them over or let the first solution stand.

admiration.why: M. Bouc and Dr Constantine marvel at Poirot's reconstruction, and the servants speak of Colonel and Sonia Armstrong with devotion.

embarrassed.why: The Countess is caught over the grease spot on her passport, Mary Debenham over the conversation Poirot overheard at Konya, and each lie exposed brings a flush.

shame.why: Pierre Michel's daughter Susanne killed herself after being accused in the Armstrong case, a shame he carries, and the conspirators flinch when their deception is laid bare.

guilt.why: The twelve feel justified rather than guilty, though Linda Arden offers to take the blame alone, and Poirot must square his conscience with letting them go.

sad.why: Linda Arden tells of Daisy, Sonia, and the colonel with tears, and the sadness of the Armstrong tragedy underlies the puzzle.

happy.why: The ending brings the conspirators relief, not happiness, and Poirot a quiet contentment with his solution.

joyful-euphoric.why: Poirot's triumph in laying out the solution is savored, but muted by the moral weight of what he has found.

effort.why: Poirot works through the night of clues, interviewing a dozen passengers, and the conspirators labored for months to plan the killing.

focused-in-flow.why: Poirot sits back, closes his eyes, and lets his little grey cells work through the evidence until the two solutions appear.

bored.why: The stalled passengers have nothing to do but wait and be questioned, and Mrs Hubbard talks to fill the hours.

distracted.why: The conspirators plant a woman in a scarlet kimono, a conductor's button, and a man with a feminine voice to lead Poirot's attention astray.

impatient.why: M. Bouc wants a culprit before the Yugoslav police arrive, and the passengers chafe at the snowbound delay.

curious.why: Poirot questions twelve passengers, examines the burnt note, the pipe cleaner, the handkerchief, and the watch, and will not rest until the whole truth is reconstructed.

surprised.why: M. Bouc and Dr Constantine are astounded as Poirot reveals that Mrs Hubbard is the actress Linda Arden and that all twelve passengers struck the blows.

awe.why: Bouc gazes at Poirot's final reconstruction with something near wonder, but nothing larger than a clever man is at work.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Poirot doubts the handkerchief and the pipe cleaner because they are too convenient, doubts every alibi confirmed by one other passenger, and doubts Hardman's credentials.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Poirot grasps at the half-remembered Armstrong case when he reads the burnt note, and senses something familiar in the Countess's face before placing it.

confused.why: Dr Constantine cannot square wounds struck by a strong right-handed man with feeble left-handed ones, and M. Bouc is lost among the contradictory clues.

frustrated.why: M. Bouc throws up his hands at a case where every clue points a different way, and Poirot complains there are too many clues.

uncertain-certain.why: Poirot moves from uncertainty to certainty by pure reasoning, then poses two solutions and leaves M. Bouc to choose which is true.

understanding.why: Poirot's final speech understands every clue at once: twelve passengers, twelve wounds, a jury's verdict carried out on a man the courts let go.

inspired.why: Poirot's insight that the clues are too many because they were planted, and Linda Arden's plan of twelve blows in the night, are the story's inspirations.

satisfied.why: Poirot lays out the complete solution with satisfaction, and having given M. Bouc his choice, declares he has the honor to retire from the case.

foreboding.why: Ratchett shows Poirot the letters threatening his life, and Poirot's refusal to protect him hangs over the night that follows.

nostalgia.why: The nurse, governess, and grandmother recall the Armstrong house before the kidnapping as a lost happy world.

anticipation-suspense.why: The conspirators wait to learn whether Poirot will expose them before the train is dug out and the Yugoslav police board.

hope.why: The twelve hope the story of a stranger who boarded at Vincovci will satisfy the police, and Poirot grants it.

schadenfreude.why: Princess Dragomiroff and the others take grim satisfaction in Cassetti's death, each having struck a blow.

elevation.why: Linda Arden offers to bear the guilt alone to spare the others, and Poirot's choice of the merciful solution ends the book on a note of moral uplift.

rage.why: Some of the twelve wounds were driven in with savage force, the rage of years finding its moment.
